newsitem.title: USA: Credit rating agencies monitor California flooding.
newsitem.headline: Credit rating agencies monitor California flooding.

text.p: Major U.S. credit rating agencies said Wednesday they were monitoring the severe flooding in California but did not expect the losses to have credit implications for hard-hit counties and cities.

California Office of Emergency Services reported Tuesday that 19 counties and one city had reported damage from the floods estimated at more than $1.5 billion. The losses included $661 million of damage to homes and businesses and $902 million of damage to infrastructure, officials said.
Standard & Poor's Corp and Moody's Investors Service Inc said they did not anticipate any flood-related rating changes.

"We're getting estimates as to what the potential costs are and how they might be covered," said S&P director Jeffrey Thiemann. "But our experience historically is that (federal and state disaster relief) agencies have been able to step in and help out."
In the near term, many cities and counties will face police and fire overtime costs that could drain their cash-strapped budgets.
Longer term, counties could face reduced property values from damage and infrastructure repair costs. The floods could also hurt employment in small farming towns, Thiemann said.
"There are bigger credit events on the horizon than this," Moody's Vice President David Brodsly said.
He added that Moody's did not expect the flooding to result in rating downgrades in the near or long term because federal and state aid would cushion the financial blow.
S&P and Moody's said it would take time to assess the situation because loss estimates were still being developed.

Twenty-three of the counties where Wilson declared states of emergency have not yet reported damage and officials said this year's floods were almost certain to overtake 1995 floods as the most damaging in state history.
The 1995 floods caused $1.8 billion of damage.
In the 19 counties reporting, 623 homes and 72 mobile homes have been destroyed and 1,895 homes suffered minor damage, the state said.

On Tuesday, California Gov. Pete Wilson called for a special session of the state Legislature "to address the clear and immediate needs of those individuals, businesses and farms victimized by those terrible floods."
The California State Association of Counties said it would lobby the Legislature to ensure that funding is provided to counties to repair damaged infrastructure.
